verdicts.why: B's mark is a stacked Langstroth hive: an outer cover, a super and a brood box with an entrance slot. That comes straight from what Dale sells and builds, and it uses flat shapes that will hold up embroidered, cut in vinyl or burned into wood. It still reads as a hive at 32 and 16 px; the cover blurs a little at 16 px but the shape stays clear. A's mark is a generic blocky M in a square frame that says nothing about bees or the river, and at 16 px it shrinks to a smudge in a box. Both set the name correctly in a similar serif and add nothing invented, so the mark decides it.

A's mark is a stacked Langstroth hive (lid, box, and a brood box with an entrance slot). It comes straight from what this client builds and sells. Its few solid blocks keep the same shape at 32 and 16 px and hold up in one color and reversed, though the thin lid softens a little at 16 px. B's mark is a blocky M in a square frame, which says nothing about bees or hives. Its M looks like a vague blob or shirt and turns into mush at 16 px. Both use the same well-set serif wordmark with the name spelled correctly, so the mark decides it.

B's mark uses O and R, the partners' surname initials, so it matches the firm's name, and its R keeps a clear bowl and leg at 16 and 32 px, in one color and reversed. A's second letter is a squared block that reads as A or H, not R, so the monogram looks like 'OA' or 'OH' and doesn't connect to 'Okafor & Reyes'. B's lockup has its own flaw: the mark is undersized next to the wordmark. Both spell the name correctly and add no invented text.

Both sheets spell the name exactly and add nothing the client didn't give, and both marks stay solid at 16 and 32 px and work in one color and reversed. The deciding problem is B's second letter: the boxy block with a notch on top and a slot below reads as 'A' or 'H', not 'R', so the monogram looks like 'OA' and points to the wrong firm. A's R has a clear bowl and leg, so 'OR' reads correctly at every size, though both are fairly generic initial monograms that don't draw on the client's own subject.

Both spell the name exactly and add nothing invented, and both use the same rounded sans in the lockup, so the choice comes down to the mark. B's otter head rising above a single waterline is one bold, simple idea that stays the same shape at 16 and 32 px and holds up cleanly in one color and reversed. A's floating otter, with its separate head, tail and wavy water, reads more like a bear in a boat, and at 16 px it breaks into fragments that would also be hard to print well on a one-color swim cap.

Both spell the name correctly and add nothing. A's mark, a round head with ears at a single waterline, keeps the same solid shape at 32 and 16 px and works in one color and reversed. B's shapes break up at small sizes: the stray vertical oval and the wave turn to noise at 16 px. B's idea also reads as a bear sitting in a boat rather than an otter swimming, while A, though plain, is one clear and well-built idea: a small animal head at the waterline.

A runs off the bottom of the page: its logo panel and its fifth section ('Use it consistently') are cut off, and it gives Bank Plaster and Cream the same hex (#FFFDF7). B fits the whole system on one page, with a logo section, a role and use for every color, a fuller contrast table, a type scale shown at size, and say/not voice pairs drawn from real brief facts. B's only flaw is a small footer slip that lists 'logo.svg, logo.svg'; neither guide invents facts.

B runs off the bottom of the page: its logo block and the final 'use it consistently' section are cut off, so the logo display and usage rules are partly lost. Its color panel also leaves a large empty area. A fits the page and gives a fuller system: logo shown on three backgrounds with a clear-space rule, a named role for every color, a full contrast table and a type scale with sizes. Its voice and imagery do/don't lists are specific to this client and match B's. A's only flaws are minor: the footer lists 'logo.svg' twice and the audience line is a little odd.

Neither page invents facts. A states every color's job in plain words (page background, cards and forms, headlines and copy, logo and actions), names the services and the nervous-adult and toddler audiences, and its larger say/skip examples are easier to read and write from. B adds useful logo variants and shows its type scale at size, but its voice and imagery text is smaller, it leaves out the services, and it leaves a large empty band at the bottom of the page.

Neither guide invents any facts, and both use nearly the same teal palette, Source Serif 4 with Public Sans, and SAY/SKIP voice examples. B wins because it gives each color a plain-language role (page background, headlines and copy, captions and labels, logo and actions, text on teal), uses the brief's services and both audiences (nervous adults and toddlers), and fills the page evenly. A leaves a large empty band at the bottom and its color roles are vaguer. A does have one advantage: it shows the reversed logo on teal, which is useful for mailers.

A's offline screen is broken: a huge empty yellow panel fills the screen and pushes the bus card off the bottom, so the parent can't see the bus's last known position.
